```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.8,
  out.width = "100%"
)

library(crossmet)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

# Reproducible illustrative observations; these are not station measurements.
set.seed(42)
dates <- seq.Date(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day")
variables <- c(
  "Temperature deg C Min", "Temperature deg C Max", "Air temp Mean",
  "Temp diff deg C", "Rainfall mm", "Soil 15cm deg C", "Soil 45cm deg C",
  "Average Wind speed Km/h", "RH (%)", "Leaf wetness (U)",
  "Lite totals daily (W/m2)"
)
sample_weather <- expand.grid(Date = dates, variable = variables) |>
  mutate(
    DOY = yday(Date),
    seasonal = 10 + 7 * sin(2 * pi * (DOY - 100) / 365),
    value = case_when(
      variable == "Temperature deg C Min" ~ seasonal - runif(n(), 1, 5),
      variable == "Temperature deg C Max" ~ seasonal + runif(n(), 2, 7),
      variable == "Air temp Mean" ~ seasonal + rnorm(n(), 0, 1),
      variable == "Temp diff deg C" ~ runif(n(), 2, 8),
      variable == "Rainfall mm" ~ rgamma(n(), shape = 1.2, scale = 2),
      variable == "Soil 15cm deg C" ~ seasonal - 1 + rnorm(n(), 0, 1),
      variable == "Soil 45cm deg C" ~ seasonal - 2 + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.7),
      variable == "Average Wind speed Km/h" ~ rgamma(n(), 3, 2),
      variable == "RH (%)" ~ pmin(100, pmax(20, rnorm(n(), 78, 12))),
      variable == "Leaf wetness (U)" ~ runif(n(), 0, 1),
      variable == "Lite totals daily (W/m2)" ~ pmax(
        0, 100 + 90 * sin(2 * pi * (DOY - 80) / 365) + rnorm(n(), 0, 20)
      ),
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  select(Date, DOY, variable, value)
```

# Plotting functions return ggplot objects

The plotting functions in **crossmet** return ordinary
`ggplot2::ggplot()` objects. This means you can save them in variables,
inspect them, and extend them with the same layers and scales you use in any
other ggplot2 workflow.

For example, create a mean air temperature plot and check its class:

```{r base-plot}
temperature_plot <- MeanAirTempPlot(sample_weather)

inherits(temperature_plot, "ggplot")
```

The result is `TRUE`: the returned object is a ggplot object, not a static
image. You can therefore add layers with the `+` operator.

# Add a geom and annotate an event

The following example adds a smoothed trend line to the daily observations.
It then marks an illustrative event date with a vertical line and a text
annotation. Replace the example date and label with an event relevant to your
own analysis (for example, a storm, frost, equipment change or management
intervention).

```{r customise-plot}
event_date <- as.Date("2024-08-15")

temperature_plot +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.numeric(event_date),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#0072B2"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = event_date,
    y = Inf,
    label = "Illustrative event",
    vjust = 1.5,
    hjust = -0.05,
    colour = "#0072B2"
  )
```

Here, `geom_smooth()` inherits the data and aesthetic mappings from the
original crossmet plot. The event marker is added as another ggplot2 layer;
`annotate()` places a label at the same date. No changes to the package
plotting function are needed.

# Extend other crossmet plots

The same approach works with the other plotting functions. For example, add a
point layer to a rainfall plot, or change its labels and theme:

```{r other-plot, eval = FALSE}
rainfall_plot <- RainfallPlot(sample_weather)

rainfall_plot +
  labs(
    title = "Daily rainfall at Crossnacreevy",
    subtitle = "Add your own explanatory subtitle",
    caption = "Source: Crossnacreevy weather observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

You can use any compatible ggplot2 layer, scale, coordinate system or theme.
For details, see the [ggplot2 documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/).
The examples in this vignette use synthetic data only and do not represent
actual station measurements.
